_readme: Fixes applied to the base source when `npm run data` builds the map (historical-basemaps to 1783; Cliopatria from 1800 to 1960). years = snapshot years (negative = BCE). n = new name, s = new 'ruled by' (null clears it), note = shown on the map as a data note. Every rule is listed on /about.

rules.name: Thai
rules.note: The source labels most of China in 2000 BCE as 'Thai'. The ancestors of the Tai peoples lived in southern China; the north was home to Longshan-era cultures and the early Erlitou (traditionally Xia) state.
rules.why: An ethnic label stretched over regions it does not describe.

rules.name: Holy Roman Empire Minor States
rules.note: The Empire's many smaller states, shown together. The Empire was dissolved in 1806.
rules.why: The Empire's smaller states, which Cliopatria draws as one.

rules.name: Cispadane Republic
rules.why: The Cispadane Republic merged into the Cisalpine Republic in 1797.

rules.name: Grand Duchy of Berg
rules.why: The Grand Duchy ended in 1813; the Congress of Vienna gave its land to Prussia.

rules.name: Nawab of Awadh
rules.why: Cliopatria names the state after its ruler's title.

rules.name: Maratha Empire
rules.note: Maratha states under the Peshwa at Pune. Defeated by the British in 1803–05, when Scindia lost Delhi, Agra and the Doab; the British ended the confederacy in 1818.
rules.why: Named as on the 1800 map.

rules.name: British Ceylon
rules.note: The Sinhalese kingdom of the island's hill country, ruled from Kandy. The British, who held the coast from 1796, took it in 1815.
rules.why: Cliopatria labels the inland kingdom, independent until 1815, as British Ceylon; the British held only the coast.

rules.name: British trading posts
rules.note: Fur-trading posts of the Hudson's Bay and North West companies, as Cliopatria draws them. First Nations held the land around them.
rules.why: Cliopatria draws these posts as part of the British Empire, with India.

rules.name: Khmer Empire
rules.note: The Khmer kingdom, under Siamese and Vietnamese overlordship.
rules.why: The Khmer Empire ended in the 15th century; by 1800 Cambodia was a smaller kingdom.

rules.name: Cambodia
rules.note: A kingdom under French protection from 1863.
rules.why: Cliopatria draws it as part of French Indochina, which was formed only in 1887.

rules.name: Qasimids
rules.why: Cliopatria names the Zaydi imamate after its ruling family.

rules.name: Karamanli Dynasty
rules.note: Ruled by the Karamanli pashas, in name for the Ottoman sultan, until 1835.
rules.why: Cliopatria names the state after its ruling family.

rules.name: Muhammad Ali dynasty
rules.note: Ruled from 1805 by Muhammad Ali, the Ottoman sultan's governor in name and Egypt's master in fact.
rules.why: Cliopatria names the state after its ruling family.

rules.name: Omani Slave Coast
rules.note: Zanzibar and the Swahili coast under the sultan of Oman, who moved his court to Zanzibar in 1840.
rules.why: Cliopatria's name for Oman's East African coast.

rules.name: House of Khalifa
rules.why: Cliopatria names the state after its ruling family.

rules.name: Merina Kingdom
rules.why: Named as OpenHistoricalMap names it.

rules.name: People's Republic of Zanzibar
rules.why: The People's Republic dates from 1964; in 1878 the sultan of Zanzibar held this coast.

rules.name: First Hellenic Republic
rules.why: The First Hellenic Republic ended in 1832; by 1878 Greece was a kingdom.

rules.name: German Africa
rules.note: The Duala kings of the Cameroon estuary. Germany made it a protectorate in 1884.
rules.why: German rule here began in 1884.

rules.name: Qatar Dynasty
rules.why: Cliopatria names the state after its ruling family.

rules.name: Comoro sultanates
rules.note: The sultanates of Anjouan, Mohéli and Grande Comore (and Mayotte, until France took it in 1841).
rules.why: Cliopatria draws these islands as part of French India or French Africa; France took Mayotte in 1841 and the rest in 1886.

rules.name: Portuguese Mozambique
rules.note: Portugal held the coast and, through its estates (prazos), the Zambezi valley; African kingdoms ruled the interior.
rules.why: Cliopatria draws it as part of the Portuguese Empire.

rules.name: South Georgia
rules.note: Claimed for Britain by James Cook in 1775; no one lived there, but sealers came.
rules.why: Cliopatria draws it as part of the British Colonial Empire.

rules.name: Saint Pierre and Miquelon
rules.note: French islands, held by Britain from 1793 to 1802.
rules.why: Cliopatria draws them as part of French Louisiana.

rules.name: Colony of Sierra Leone
rules.note: Freetown and its peninsula, settled by freed slaves from 1787 and run by the Sierra Leone Company until it became a crown colony in 1808.
rules.why: Cliopatria draws it as part of the British Cape Colony.

rules.name: Colony of Sierra Leone
rules.note: Freetown and its peninsula, a crown colony since 1808.
rules.why: Cliopatria draws it as part of the British Cape Colony.

rules.name: Lagos Colony
rules.note: Lagos and its coast, a British colony from 1861, run with the Gold Coast from 1874 to 1886.
rules.why: Cliopatria draws it as part of the British Gold Coast.

rules.name: Fernando Po
rules.note: Spain's by treaty since 1778; its settlers left in 1781, and the Bubi people held the island.
rules.why: Cliopatria draws it as part of the Spanish Empire.

rules.name: Prince of Wales Island
rules.note: Penang, which the East India Company took from the sultan of Kedah in 1786; the strip of mainland opposite (Province Wellesley) was added in 1800.
rules.why: Cliopatria draws it as part of the British Colonial Empire.

rules.name: Malacca
rules.note: A Dutch colony, held by Britain from 1795 to 1818; the Dutch traded it to Britain for good in 1824.
rules.why: Cliopatria draws it as part of the British Colonial Empire.

rules.name: Malacca
rules.note: A Dutch colony, held by Britain from 1795 to 1818; the Dutch traded it to Britain for good in 1824.
rules.why: Cliopatria draws it as part of the Dutch East Indies.

rules.name: Padang
rules.note: The Dutch posts on Sumatra's west coast around Padang, held by Britain from 1795 to 1819.
rules.why: Cliopatria draws it as part of the British Colonial Empire.

rules.name: Padang
rules.note: The Dutch posts on Sumatra's west coast around Padang, held by Britain from 1795 to 1819.
rules.why: Cliopatria draws it as part of the Dutch East Indies.

rules.name: Amboyna and Banda
rules.note: The Dutch spice islands of Ambon and Banda, with Buru, Seram and the islands to the south-east, taken by Britain in 1796 and handed back in 1803 after the Peace of Amiens.
rules.why: Cliopatria draws them as part of the Dutch East Indies.

rules.name: Bangka and Belitung
rules.note: Ceded to Britain in 1812 by the sultan it had put on Palembang's throne. Under the treaty of 1814 Britain traded them to the Netherlands for Cochin, in India, and handed them over in 1816.
rules.why: Cliopatria draws Bangka as part of the Dutch East Indies and Belitung as part of the British Colonial Empire.

rules.name: Makassar
rules.note: The Dutch government of Makassar in southern Celebes, which passed to Britain with Java in 1811; handed back to the Netherlands in 1816.
rules.why: Cliopatria draws it as part of the Dutch East Indies.

rules.name: Kupang
rules.note: The Dutch post at Kupang on Timor, which surrendered to Britain in January 1812; handed back to the Netherlands in 1816.
rules.why: Cliopatria draws it as part of the Dutch East Indies.

rules.name: Moluccas
rules.note: The Dutch spice islands (Ambon, Banda, Ternate and their dependencies, with Manado in Celebes), taken by Britain in 1810 and handed back to the Netherlands in 1817.
rules.why: Cliopatria draws them as part of the Dutch East Indies.

rules.name: North Borneo
rules.note: Leased from the sultans of Brunei and Sulu in 1877–78 by Alfred Dent’s company, which Britain chartered as the British North Borneo Company in 1881.
rules.why: Cliopatria draws it as part of the British Colonial Empire.

rules.name: Martinique
rules.note: A French colony, held by Britain from 1794 to 1802.
rules.why: Cliopatria draws it as part of the British Colonial Empire.

rules.name: Martinique
rules.note: Returned to France in 1814. During Napoleon’s Hundred Days in 1815 British troops occupied it, staying until 1816.
rules.why: Cliopatria draws it as part of the Bourbon Kingdom of France.

rules.name: Colony of Guadeloupe
rules.note: Returned to France in 1814. During Napoleon’s Hundred Days in 1815 British troops occupied it, staying until 1816.
rules.why: Cliopatria draws it as part of the Bourbon Kingdom of France.

rules.name: Commonwealth of Australia
rules.why: Named as on the later maps.

rules.name: La Réunion
rules.why: Named as on the other maps of these years.

rules.name: Portuguese Republic
rules.why: Cliopatria's name for Portugal; its pieces here are the Azores and Madeira, part of Portugal.

rules.name: Estado Novo
rules.why: Cliopatria's name for Portugal under Salazar (from 1933); its pieces here are Portugal's islands. Its colonies are named on their own.

rules.name: Denmark-Norway
rules.why: Cliopatria's name for Denmark, which had not been joined to Norway since 1814.

rules.name: Second Spanish Republic
rules.why: Cliopatria draws the Canary Islands as the Republic's; the Nationalists held them from July 1936. Spain is shown whole on this map.

rules.name: Francoist Spain
rules.why: Cliopatria's name for Spain under Franco; its pieces here are the Canary Islands, part of Spain.

rules.name: French Fourth Republic
rules.why: Cliopatria's name for France, ahead of the Fourth Republic's founding in October 1946.

rules.name: French Fifth Republic
rules.why: Cliopatria's name for France; its overseas departments and territories are named on their own.

rules.name: United States of America
rules.why: Named as on the other maps of these years.

rules.name: North Yemen
rules.why: The Mutawakkilite Kingdom of Yemen; 'North Yemen' dates from 1962.

rules.name: Comoros
rules.note: Part of the colony of Madagascar until 1946, when the islands became a French overseas territory of their own.
rules.why: Cliopatria draws them as part of French Africa.

rules.name: Curaçao
rules.note: A Dutch colony, held by Britain from 1800 to 1803 and from 1807 to 1816.
rules.why: Cliopatria draws it as part of the British Colonial Empire.

rules.name: French Egypt
rules.note: An Ottoman province, occupied by Napoleon’s army from 1798 until it surrendered in 1801.
rules.why: Cliopatria draws it as part of the French Consulate.

rules.name: Konbaung Dynasty
rules.why: Cliopatria names the kingdom after its ruling dynasty.

rules.name: Duchy of Bavaria
rules.why: Bavaria’s rulers had been electors of the Holy Roman Empire since 1623.

rules.name: Dutch Gold Coast
rules.why: Cliopatria gives the Dutch forts no ruler.

rules.name: Dutch Gold Coast
rules.why: Cliopatria gives the Dutch forts no ruler.

rules.name: Luisiana
rules.why: France ceded Louisiana to Spain in 1762; it went back to France secretly in 1800.

rules.name: Zhoa
rules.why: The Shang dynasty ruled the Yellow River valley c. 1600–1046 BCE; the Zhou came later.

rules.name: Zhoa
rules.why: Misspelling of Zhou (dynasty from 1046 BCE).

rules.name: Hittites
rules.why: The Hittite Empire collapsed around 1180 BCE; small Neo-Hittite kingdoms survived in Syria and Anatolia.

rules.name: Urartu
rules.note: Urartu only emerged around 860 BCE. Earlier, this highland was home to Hurrian peoples (the Mitanni kingdom in 1500 BCE).
rules.why: Urartu appears centuries before it existed.

rules.name: Xiongnu
rules.note: The Xiongnu confederation formed around 209 BCE; in 400 BCE these steppes were held by earlier nomadic peoples.
rules.why: Xiongnu shown about 200 years early.

rules.name: Kushan Empire
rules.why: The Kushan Empire was founded by the Yuezhi around 30 CE.

rules.name: Mauryan Empire
rules.note: The Mauryan Empire fell around 185 BCE. Its successor, the Shunga Empire, was much smaller than the outline shown here.
rules.why: Mauryan Empire shown about 85 years after it fell.

rules.name: Seleucid Kingdom
rules.note: By 100 BCE the Seleucids held little beyond Syria; Parthia had taken Mesopotamia and Iran. The source outline is too large.
rules.why: Outline far larger than Seleucid territory in 100 BCE.

rules.name: Parthian Empire
rules.why: The Sasanians overthrew the Parthians in 224 CE.

rules.name: Persia
rules.why: Persia in 400 CE was the Sasanian Empire.

rules.name: Suren Kingdom
rules.note: The Indo-Parthian (Suren) kingdom had ended by the late 1st century CE; the source keeps it too long.
rules.why: Kingdom shown long after it ended.

rules.name: Satavahanihara
rules.note: The Satavahana dynasty ended around 220 CE; by 300 the Deccan was split among successor states.
rules.why: Dynasty shown after it ended.

rules.name: Jin Empire
rules.why: The Jin dynasty ended in 420; southern China was ruled by the Southern Qi (479–502).

rules.name: Sui Empire
rules.note: Empress Wu Zetian ruled under the name 'Zhou' from 690 to 705, between Tang reigns.
rules.why: The Sui dynasty ended in 618.

rules.name: Sasanian Empire
rules.why: The Sasanian Empire fell to the Arab conquests by 651.

rules.name: Sasanian dependencies
rules.note: The Sasanian Empire had fallen by 651; these lands were ruled by local dynasties or the Caliphate.
rules.why: Shown as Sasanian after the empire fell.

rules.name: Western Gokturk Khaganate
rules.why: The Western Turkic Khaganate fell to the Tang in 657; the Türgesh dominated the region by 699.

rules.name: Koguryo
rules.why: Goguryeo fell in 668; Balhae was founded in its northern lands in 698.

rules.name: Yamato
rules.why: The Yamato period ended in 710.

rules.name: Denmark-Norway
rules.note: Denmark and Norway were not one kingdom in 1000. Denmark's Sweyn Forkbeard controlled much of Norway after the Battle of Svolder (1000); the lasting union dates from 1380. Greenland was a self-governing Norse settlement.
rules.why: Union shown centuries early.

rules.name: Xixia
rules.note: The Western Xia state was proclaimed in 1038; in 1000 this was Tangut territory under Song and Liao influence.
rules.why: Western Xia shown before it was founded.

rules.name: Mongol Empire
rules.why: Temüjin was proclaimed Genghis Khan, founding the Mongol Empire, in 1206.

rules.name: Liao
rules.note: The Liao dynasty fell in 1125. In 1200 northern China was ruled by the Jurchen Jin dynasty, which this source does not draw.
rules.why: Liao shown 75 years after it fell; Jin missing.

rules.name: Fatimid Caliphate
rules.why: Saladin ended the Fatimid Caliphate in 1171.

rules.name: Ghaznavid Emirate
rules.why: The Ghurids took the last Ghaznavid lands in 1186.

rules.name: Sultanate of Delhi
rules.why: The Delhi Sultanate was founded in 1206; in 1200 northern India was ruled by the Ghurids.

rules.name: Buwayhid Emirates
rules.note: The Buyid emirates ended in 1062. In 1200 this region was held by Seljuk successor states and the Khwarazmians.
rules.why: Buyids shown long after they ended.

rules.name: Tibet
rules.why: Yuan (Mongol) control of Tibet ended in 1354.

rules.name: Novgorod
rules.why: The Mongol Empire no longer existed as one state in 1400.

rules.name: Inca Empire
rules.why: The last Inca state fell in 1572.

rules.name: Songhai
rules.note: The Songhai Empire fell to Morocco in 1591. This area was then split between the Moroccan Pashalik of Timbuktu and smaller successor states; the source keeps the old outline.
rules.why: Empire shown after its conquest.

rules.name: Vijayanagara
rules.note: The Vijayanagara Empire ended in 1646; its lands passed to Nayak successor states and the Deccan sultanates.
rules.why: Empire shown after it ended.

rules.name: Dutch Brazil
rules.why: The Dutch were expelled from Brazil in 1654.

rules.name: Austrian Empire
rules.why: The Austrian Empire was only proclaimed in 1804.

rules.name: Dutch East Indies
rules.why: Typo in the source ('Neterlands').

rules.name: Quebec
rules.why: France ceded Canada to Britain in 1763.

rules.name: Papua New Guinea
rules.why: Papua New Guinea became a country in 1975.

geometry.what: Drew the 1994, 2000 and 2010 maps from Natural Earth’s present-day borders, rolled back to 31 December of each year: South Sudan joined to Sudan (independent 2011), Crimea to Ukraine (annexed by Russia in 2014), Serbia, Montenegro and Kosovo as Yugoslavia in 1994 and 2000, the Netherlands Antilles (dissolved 2010), East Timor under UN administration in 2000 and held by Indonesia in 1994, Zaire (renamed in 1997), British Hong Kong and Portuguese Macau in 1994, and the names countries had then (Turkey, Macedonia, Swaziland, Czech Republic, Cape Verde).
geometry.why: The historical source’s outlines for these years were coarse and out of date: Bratislava was drawn inside Austria, Kosovo and East Timor were missing after independence, Walvis Bay was still South African, and several island countries were not mapped. Dates checked against CShapes 2.0 (ETH Zurich).

geometry.what: Drew Europe’s national borders from HistoGIS (Austrian Academy of Sciences), which takes them from maps of the time: for example Alsace-Lorraine in Germany, Bessarabia in Russia, Finland, Iceland and the Caucasus within the empires that held them, Southern Dobruja Bulgarian in 1900 and Romanian in 1914. Cyprus in 1900 and 1914 is shown as Ottoman land under British administration.
geometry.why: The historical source’s European borders were approximate; in 1914 it showed Finland, Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan as independent and Austria-Hungary about 4% too small. HistoGIS is published under CC BY 4.0.

geometry.what: Drew Europe’s national borders from OpenHistoricalMap, which dates every border change to the day: for example Finland’s border before 1940 (Vyborg and Petsamo Finnish), Estonia’s and Latvia’s pre-war borders, the Free City of Danzig (1920–1938), the Memel Territory under Allied rule (1920), the Saar under the League of Nations (1920, 1930), Alsace-Lorraine French again, Italian Istria and Zadar, Czechoslovakia after the Munich Agreement and Hungary after the First Vienna Award (1938), the Hatay State (1938) and Poland’s borders after 1945. The same source gives the French zone of Morocco, so Spain’s zone shows apart from it (1920–1945), and Manchukuo (1938).
geometry.why: The historical source’s European borders were approximate: in 1920 it showed Strasbourg as German and Vyborg as Russian, and in 1938 Danzig as Polish. OpenHistoricalMap is public domain (CC0); every border was checked against CShapes 2.0 (ETH Zurich) and agrees to within a few percent, except where CShapes keeps a border that had not yet changed in law.

geometry.what: Drew the maps from 1800 to 1960 from Cliopatria (Seshat Global History Databank), cut to Natural Earth’s coastline, with OpenHistoricalMap’s dated borders laid over it and HistoGIS’s in Europe from 1815 to 1914, instead of the historical-basemaps source. Where one source keeps a single outline for decades while the borders moved, the other’s dated outline is used: in India, Cliopatria’s Awadh in 1800 and Maratha Confederacy in 1815. A few places are set from Natural Earth’s outlines or Cliopatria’s: Bombay and Surat as British in 1800, the Mughal emperor’s Delhi in 1815, Bulgaria and Eastern Rumelia in 1878–80, the Falklands, and, approximately, Cutch and the Ahom kingdom of Assam. From 1900 OpenHistoricalMap also gives territories it files below the country level: Papua and New Guinea under Australia, the Far Eastern Republic and the Soviet republics of 1920, Khiva and Bukhara under Russian protection (1900, 1914), the Lado Enclave (1900), the protectorates of French Indochina (1920–1938), Berlin’s sectors (1945) and West Berlin (1960), and Dadra and Nagar Haveli (1960). Cliopatria’s scattered pieces of an empire are named as the colonies they were (Algeria, Senegal, Martinique, Portuguese Mozambique; in 1960 France’s overseas departments and territories and Portugal’s colonies), and the lands Japan occupied in the war are drawn under their own rulers in 1945.
geometry.why: These sources date their borders to the year and allow any use with credit.

geometry.what: Redrew Africa as it was divided between colonies, which had mostly drawn today’s borders by 1900 (shown with Natural Earth’s outlines, some by province), with the states still ruling themselves: Ethiopia, Liberia, Morocco, Darfur, Wadai, and the Boer republics at war with Britain. Also corrected Siam with the lands it ceded in 1904–1909, Chile with the Atacama coast and Tacna, Bolivia with Acre, Peru, Ecuador, Colombia and Paraguay with today’s borders where the sources draw overlapping claims, Spain’s Río de Oro south of 26°N, British Guiana’s 1899 border, Bulgaria with Eastern Rumelia, the United States’ new Philippines, Hawaii, Puerto Rico and Cuba, Japanese Taiwan, Portuguese Timor, Sarawak and North Borneo, New Zealand, Newfoundland, and Australia’s six colonies on the eve of federation.
geometry.why: The source showed much of Africa as peoples and kingdoms that colonial armies had already conquered (Samori Touré’s empire in 1898, the Ndebele kingdom in 1893, Benin in 1897), left large areas unnamed and still showed Harar as Egyptian, 15 years after Egypt left. Elsewhere it kept borders from before the War of the Pacific (1879–1884) and Spain’s colonies after 1898.

geometry.what: Gave land drawn for the wrong country to the country that held it, using Natural Earth’s outlines of today’s borders and provinces: Turkey within its 1923 Lausanne borders in 1920 (no Sèvres zones), Greece with its Aegean islands in 1920, Tacna Chilean in 1914 (until 1929), Hatay to French Syria until 1938 (the State of Aleppo in 1920), Yemen and the British Aden Protectorate as separate states (from 1900), Transjordan apart from Iraq, Iraq independent in 1938, Saudi Arabia’s borders in 1930 and 1938 (no Ha’il emirate after 1921), Egypt and Libya with today’s border in 1914 and 1920, French Equatorial Africa apart from French West Africa in 1914, Angola’s eastern border as arbitrated in 1905 (1914), the Spanish Sahara south of 27°40′N with Spain’s zones in Morocco and Ifni (Spanish from 1934), Laos and Cambodia (1920–1938), the Byelorussian SSR around Minsk (1920), Thailand without the Malay and Shan lands it gave back in 1945, Italian Somaliland and British Jubaland in 1914, Jubaland British until 1925, British (Southern) Cameroons, Korea and Taiwan as Japanese colonies (1914–1938), Sarawak and North Borneo with today’s border with Dutch Borneo, Zanzibar, Hawaii (until statehood in 1959), Newfoundland apart from Canada, Cyprus as a British colony (1920–1945), Portuguese Timor, Trieste Italian in 1945 (run by the Allies from June 1945, Italian in law until 1947), Upper Volta split between its neighbours in 1945, Lebanon and North Yemen’s borders in 1945 and 1960, Peru, Ecuador and Colombia with today’s borders to 1938, and Paraguay’s in the Chaco to 1930 (close to the lines each held; the sources draw each country’s whole claim), and in 1960 the West Bank to Jordan, Gaza to Egypt, South Vietnam, Dutch New Guinea, Singapore and Hawaii (a US state from 1959). Colonies whose borders have not changed since (Gambia, Basutoland, Swaziland, Brunei, Portuguese and Spanish Guinea, Puerto Rico, Togo, Haiti from 1938) now follow today’s lines, Islands and small states the sources left blank or gave to a neighbour were added: the Solomon Islands, New Caledonia, the Bahamas, Jamaica, Trinidad, Cape Verde and Réunion; the Isle of Man, Malta, Liechtenstein, Andorra and San Marino on every map from 1900; the Dodecanese under Italian (1938) and British (1945) rule; and in 1945 and 1960 the Faroes and the Baltic coast and islands (Soviet from 1944), with Germany’s islands by occupation zone in 1945.
geometry.why: Each map was checked against CShapes 2.0 (ETH Zurich) on its date (31 December, or 28 June for 1914), and these were the places where the source drew land for a country that did not hold it.

geometry.what: Removed the thin strips of a shape’s old outline left along a new border or coastline: at sea they go, on land they go to the neighbours. For example, the source’s British Somaliland showed as a strip along the Italian coast in 1914.
geometry.why: Where a better outline replaced the source’s, the old shape could show through as thin strips of the wrong colour.

geometry.what: Split the 'Great Khanate' into the Ming Empire (outline from the 1492 snapshot) and the Northern Yuan.
geometry.why: The Ming dynasty had ruled China since 1368; the source still drew the Mongol Yuan state.

geometry.what: Separated Svalbard from Norway / Denmark-Norway / Sweden–Norway.
geometry.why: Svalbard belonged to no country until the 1920 Svalbard Treaty, which took effect in 1925.

geometry.what: Separated Crimea from Russia as its own disputed shape.
geometry.why: Russia has controlled Crimea since 2014, but most UN members recognize it as part of Ukraine.

geometry.what: Gave the blank strips along coasts to the shapes beside them: thin strips (up to about 20 km wide) everywhere, and every strip along Australia's coast. A strip that borders several shapes is shared out, each part going to the nearest, and merged into its shape rather than added as a separate piece (which drew the old coastline through the country, and ran Libya along Egypt's coast from 1914). In 1600–1815 the thin coastal slivers of the older 'Australian aboriginal hunter-gatherers' shape go to the nations beside them the same way.
geometry.why: The source's outlines often stop short of the real coastline, so strips of land showed as 'not mapped' between its shapes and the sea (in Australia from 1600, also as slivers of the older shape the source still draws underneath the nations).

geometry.what: Gave thin unnamed slivers wedged between two or more neighbours (up to about 30 km wide, with no coast) to the neighbour each shares most border with. For example, a 29,000 km² wedge south of Great Slave Lake in 900.
geometry.why: Where the source's outlines of neighbours don't quite meet, the gap between them showed as 'not mapped'. Wider unclaimed areas stay as the source draws them.

geometry.what: Filled land the source leaves blank (for example Sumbawa in Indonesia) as 'not mapped in the source', so the map has no false sea.
geometry.why: Islands and coasts missing from the historical outlines.
